title: Large Area Real-Space Crystallography and Thickness Determination of Mesoscopic Semiconductor Membranes Using Zone Axis Patterns and Correlative SEM-S/TEM Modes
content: Structural and dimensional characterization of layered structures in semiconductors is increasingly important for microelectronics and nanoelectronics manufacturing because of the continuing downward scaling of device dimensions. Manufacturers require low-uncertainty, non-destructive metrology to determine local crystal symmetry, orientation, defects, layer thickness, and topography with high spatial resolution over large areas. Scanning and transmission electron microscopy (S/TEM) are widely employed to ensure that the structural uniformity and device dimensions enable the desired functionality and performance. Electron diffraction (ED) techniques in S/TEMs with an incident beam oriented along a lattice direction parallel to a high-symmetry major zone axis are often used to characterize the crystal symmetry, orientation, defects, and thickness of silicon on insulators and related layered semiconductor structures. When layer thickness increases above approximately 100 nm, interference of dynamically diffracted beams may result in the formation of real-space zone axis patterns (ZAPs) that exhibit complex symmetric intensity distributions like those observed with convergent-beam ED (CBED) patterns [1-4]. ZAPs, therefore, allow direct crystallographic analysis of the examined area [1]. ZAPs are usually observed over a few micrometers in images of foils symmetrically bent near the zone axis [2-4]. Here, we report on the observation of ZAPs over much larger areas in unbent, flat specimens due to the varying angle between incident electrons within the converging beam. The flatness of suspended mesoscopic single crystal Si membranes was enhanced by a strain-compensating silicon nitride frame at its perimeter to avoid buckling (Figs. 1a and 1b). Correlative field emission SEM (FESEM) and bright field/dark field (BF/DF) S/TEM measurements were performed using custom single-tilt holders capable of accommodating membranes with 5 mm × 5 mm frames. The ZAPs observed in low-magnification S/TEM modes (Fig. 2a) represented crystal orientation maps near the [001] zone axis. The ZAPs were collected over circular saucer-like membrane areas with up to 0.9 mm field of view being terminated at the Si-Si3N4 interface. The spatial extent of ZAPs, in this case, was two orders of magnitude larger than for typical previously observed patterns of bent foils [1-4]. Moreover, the ZAP in Fig. 2a remarkably resembles the symmetry of corresponding large-angle CBED (LACBED) patterns (Fig. 2b). This demonstrates the high structural uniformity of the membranes. In line with these findings, only fine-scale roughness features with lateral size in the approximate range from 2 nm to 5 nm likely induced by uneven Si etching during fabrication and near the Si-Si3N4 interface were revealed by high-resolution TEM (not shown). Employing a Bloch wave simulation method [4-6], a series of LACBED patterns involving multiple excited Bragg beams were computed for our operating conditions with Si window thicknesses varying from 175 nm to 274 nm by a 1 nm step. The computations (Fig. 2c) showed that the shapes of the Bragg reflection features and the number of Pendellösung fringes strongly depend on the membrane thickness. The measurements best matched the Bloch wave simulations at 210 nm, while the simulations at 5 nm below and above this value already revealed noticeable deviations from the experimental patterns in the number and contrast of the fringes and features. The membrane thickness derived in this way was corroborated by determining the total membrane thickness using an electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) log-ratio technique (Figs. 3a and 3b). The average local thickness determined by EELS near the center of the membrane was approximately t=220nm, which is in good agreement considering the uncertainty of the log-ratio method estimated from the difference between the experimental and calculated values of the inelastic mean free path for silicon is less than 0.1t at the 95 % coverage interval [7-10]. This uncertainty derives from approximations used to estimate the inelastic mean free path and is systematic for a given material. The EELS thickness increased to approximately 250 nm near the Si-Si3N4 interface, as profiled in Fig. 3. We intend to employ correlative SEM-S/TEM to aid model-based multiscale nondestructive diagnostics, topography, and thickness profiling of reference structures patterned on membranes that can improve the accuracy of metrology methods to be used for next-generation electronic device development and manufacturing.
